items.prompt: What is the first line of defence that your body uses against microbes?

options.label: The skin and the lining of your internal surfaces
options.feedback: Correct. The skin and the mucous membranes that line your nose, mouth, and airways act as a physical barrier that stops most microbes from getting in.

options.label: White blood cells that eat microbes
options.feedback: White blood cells are part of the second line of defence, which only acts after a microbe has already gotten past the skin or linings.

options.label: The fever your body raises when you are ill
options.feedback: A fever is a later response that happens after an infection has already begun, not the first barrier that stops microbes from entering.

options.label: The acid in your stomach
options.feedback: Stomach acid is a chemical barrier, but it only protects one specific entry point (the digestive tract), not the whole body like the skin does.

items.ok_line: Your skin and linings are the first defence against microbes.
items.ko_line: That response comes later in the defence process, not first.
items.exp_text: The skin covers the outside of your body, and the mucous membranes line the inside surfaces that open to the outside, like your nose and mouth. Together they form a continuous physical barrier that most microbes cannot cross while it is unbroken.

items.prompt: What does the mucus in your nose and airways do to help protect you?

options.label: It kills all microbes instantly
options.feedback: Mucus does not kill all microbes. It traps many of them so they cannot move deeper, but some microbes can still survive in mucus.

options.label: It traps microbes and stops them from reaching your lungs
options.feedback: Correct. Mucus is sticky, so it catches microbes and dust. Tiny hairs in your airways then push the mucus upward so it can be swallowed or coughed out.

options.label: It makes your nose warmer so microbes die
options.feedback: Warmth alone does not kill most microbes, and the main role of mucus is trapping, not heating. Your nose warms air for other reasons.

options.label: It dries out the inside of your nose
options.feedback: Mucus is the opposite of dry; it is wet and sticky. Drying would actually make the lining less effective at trapping microbes.

items.ok_line: Mucus catches microbes before they reach the lungs.
items.ko_line: That describes a different function or a wrong effect.
items.exp_text: Mucus is a sticky liquid produced by cells in your nose and airways. It catches microbes and dust particles as you breathe in, and the cilia (tiny hair-like parts) move the mucus up and out, so the trapped microbes cannot travel down into your lungs.

items.prompt: Which part of your body produces tears that help wash microbes away from your eyes?

options.label: The nose
options.feedback: The nose produces mucus, not tears. Tears come from glands located near the eyes, not from the nasal passages.

options.label: The skin around the eye
options.feedback: The skin itself does not produce tears. Tears are made by special glands that lie just above and to the side of each eye.

options.label: The tear glands near the eye
options.feedback: Correct. Tear glands, also called lacrimal glands, sit above each eye and release tears that flow across the eye surface and drain into the nose.

options.label: The eyelid
options.feedback: The eyelid spreads tears across the eye, but it does not make them. The actual production happens in the tear glands.

items.ok_line: Tears come from glands near each eye.
items.ko_line: That structure does not produce tears.
items.exp_text: Tear glands sit in the upper outer corner of each eye socket. They release a continuous flow of tears that washes over the front of the eye, carrying away microbes and small particles, and also contains a chemical that can kill some microbes.

items.prompt: What happens to microbes that are swallowed along with your saliva?

options.label: They multiply in your stomach
options.feedback: Most microbes cannot multiply in the stomach because the strong acid there kills them or stops them from growing.

options.label: They enter your bloodstream directly from the stomach
options.feedback: The stomach lining is a barrier too, and the acid kills most microbes before they can get through it. They do not pass straight into the blood.

options.label: They stay alive and cause a stomach infection every time
options.feedback: Swallowing saliva is normal and safe. The acid in the stomach neutralizes most of the microbes you swallow, so they do not normally cause illness.

options.label: They are mostly destroyed by the acid in your stomach
options.feedback: Correct. The stomach produces a very strong acid that kills most microbes that come in with food, drink, or swallowed mucus from the airways.

items.ok_line: Swallowed microbes are mostly killed by stomach acid.
items.ko_line: That is not what actually happens to swallowed microbes.
items.exp_text: Your stomach secretes hydrochloric acid, which creates a very hostile environment for microbes. Anything you swallow, including saliva that has trapped microbes from your nose and throat, is bathed in this acid and most of the microbes are destroyed before they can go further.

items.prompt: What is the role of white blood cells in defending your body?

options.label: They attack and destroy microbes that have gotten past the skin
options.feedback: Correct. White blood cells are the main cellular defenders. Some engulf microbes directly, and others produce antibodies that help destroy them.

options.label: They form a physical barrier like the skin
options.feedback: White blood cells float in your blood and tissues; they do not form a continuous covering. The skin is the physical barrier, not the cells.

options.label: They lower your body temperature to stop microbes
options.feedback: White blood cells do not lower temperature. In fact, they trigger a fever, which raises temperature to help fight infection.

options.label: They repair wounds by turning into new skin cells
options.feedback: White blood cells help clean wounds and fight infection, but they do not become skin cells. New skin cells come from the skin itself.

items.ok_line: White blood cells hunt and destroy invading microbes.
items.ko_line: That describes a different defence or a different cell type.
items.exp_text: White blood cells are produced in your bone marrow and travel in your blood. When they detect a microbe that has entered your body, they move to the site, swallow the microbe, or release chemicals that kill it. Some also produce antibodies that stick to the microbe and mark it for destruction.

items.prompt: What causes a fever when you catch an infection?

options.label: The microbes themselves heat up the body
options.feedback: Microbes do not heat your body directly. The fever comes from your own body's response, not from the microbes generating heat.

options.label: The body raises its temperature to help fight the microbes
options.feedback: Correct. When white blood cells detect microbes, they release chemicals that tell the brain to raise the body's set temperature. This higher temperature slows microbe growth and helps immune cells work better.

options.label: The skin produces extra heat from friction
options.feedback: Skin friction is not involved in fever. The heat comes from internal responses, not from rubbing or friction on the skin.

options.label: The body tries to cool down the infection site
options.feedback: A fever is a warming response, not a cooling one. The body raises temperature all over, not just at one spot.

items.ok_line: Your body raises its temperature on purpose to fight infection.
items.ko_line: That does not explain where the heat comes from.
items.exp_text: When white blood cells encounter microbes, they release chemicals called pyrogens. These travel to the brain and reset the body's thermostat to a higher level. The body then starts shivering and conserving heat to reach that new, higher temperature, which makes it harder for the infection to spread.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of pain after an injury like touching something too hot?

options.label: To make you cry so tears can wash the wound
options.feedback: Tears are for eye infections, not for injuries elsewhere. Pain's main job is not to produce tears, but to warn you.

options.label: To force you to sleep so the body can heal
options.feedback: Sleep helps healing, but pain itself does not cause sleep. Pain keeps you aware and prompts you to remove the cause of harm.

options.label: To warn you to move away from the danger
options.feedback: Correct. Pain is a warning signal. It tells you something is damaging your body, so you pull away quickly and avoid further harm.

options.label: To make the injured area swell so blood can clot
options.feedback: Swelling comes from inflammation, not from pain itself. Pain does not cause swelling; it only signals that damage has occurred.

items.ok_line: Pain tells you to remove the source of harm.
items.ko_line: That effect is caused by something else, not by pain.
items.exp_text: Pain is produced by nerve endings that detect damage or danger. When you touch something too hot, the pain makes you jerk your hand away instantly, which prevents a worse burn. It also reminds you to protect the injured area while it heals.

items.prompt: What is the function of a scab that forms over a healing wound?

options.label: It provides a food source for white blood cells
options.feedback: Scabs are made of dried blood and clotting material, not food. White blood cells do not eat scabs; they eat microbes.

options.label: It makes the wound heal faster by pulling the edges together
options.feedback: The scab does not pull the edges. New skin cells grow underneath the scab, but the scab itself is a protective cover, not a clamp.

options.label: It keeps the wound moist so bacteria can grow easily
options.feedback: That would be harmful. The scab actually keeps the wound dry and sealed, which prevents bacteria from entering, not the opposite.

options.label: It seals the wound to keep microbes out while new skin grows underneath
options.feedback: Correct. A scab is a dried clot that covers the cut. It blocks microbes from entering and gives the new skin cells below time to grow and close the gap.

items.ok_line: The scab blocks microbes while skin regrows beneath it.
items.ko_line: That is not what a scab does for the healing wound.
items.exp_text: When you cut yourself, blood clots quickly at the wound. The clot dries and hardens into a scab, which acts like a natural bandage. It keeps out dirt and microbes, and it holds the wound closed. Underneath, new skin grows across, and the scab eventually falls off when it is no longer needed.

items.prompt: Why does a lymph node in your neck sometimes swell when you are fighting an infection?

options.label: It is where the infection itself grows
options.feedback: Lymph nodes are not where the infection grows; they filter microbes out of the lymph. Swelling happens because they are working, not because the microbe is actually living in the node.

options.label: It is full of white blood cells fighting the infection
options.feedback: Correct. Lymph nodes contain many white blood cells. When microbes are trapped there, the white cells multiply and attack them, making the node enlarge.

options.label: It is filling up with extra blood to heal the area
options.feedback: Lymph nodes filter lymph fluid, not blood. They do not store extra blood; the swelling comes from an increase in immune cells.

options.label: It is producing antibodies that circulate in the blood
options.feedback: Lymph nodes do produce antibodies, but the swelling is not a sign of antibody production alone; it is the accumulation of white blood cells doing the work.

items.ok_line: Swollen lymph nodes mean white blood cells are fighting there.
items.ko_line: That is not what happens inside a swollen node.
items.exp_text: Lymph nodes sit along your lymphatic system, which drains fluid from tissues. As lymph passes through, microbes are filtered out and trapped inside the node. White blood cells there recognise the microbes, multiply, and start attacking, which causes the node to grow larger and feel tender.

items.prompt: What substance in your blood helps stop bleeding from a small cut within a few minutes?

options.label: Platelets that form a clot
options.feedback: Correct. Platelets are tiny cell fragments in your blood. They stick to the cut, clump together, and help form a clot that plugs the break in the blood vessel.

options.label: White blood cells that eat the broken tissue
options.feedback: White blood cells fight infection, but they do not stop bleeding. They arrive later to clean up microbes, not to clot blood.

options.label: Red blood cells that carry oxygen and seal the cut
options.feedback: Red blood cells carry oxygen, but they do not form clots. The sealing is done by platelets and a protein called fibrin.

options.label: Plasma that evaporates and leaves a solid plug
options.feedback: Plasma is the liquid part of blood; it does not evaporate to form a plug. Clotting is an active chemical process, not simple evaporation.

items.ok_line: Platelets clump and form a clot to seal the cut.
items.ko_line: That blood component does not cause clotting.
items.exp_text: When a blood vessel is cut, platelets in the blood become activated at the wound. They stick to the exposed tissue and to each other, forming a temporary plug. Then a protein called fibrin forms a mesh that strengthens the plug into a solid clot, which stops the bleeding and becomes the base for a scab.
